extracted.intended_audience: patent agents / patent attorneys (drafting patent claims), e.g., European practice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting patent claims: how to prepare claims (timing, form, wording), ensure support in the specification, choose claim scope and categories, and handle prosecution and exclusions across jurisdictions. Focused on practical techniques used by patent practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims as the heart and scope of the application
rubrics_metrics.description: The Claims represent the heart of the patent application and define the scope of protection given to an invention; they are usually the first and sometimes the only parts of the patent application actually reviewed by the patent examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims carefully because they legally determine protection; anticipate examiner focus and third‑party scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare draft claims first and iterate
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare draft claims for the invention as the first step. Write draft claims before preparing the description, drawings, etc., and discuss the draft claims with the inventor early in the drafting process. Review/revise the claims again once the specification has been completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch draft claims during disclosure meetings for immediate inventor feedback; claims drafted early reveal which terms need clear description in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a "picture claim" in initial drafts
rubrics_metrics.description: In the initial draft claims, the patent agent may wish to use a “picture” claim which essentially “draws a picture” of the invention in words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A picture claim is not typically the broadest claim and does not use highly abstract language, but it is helpful in beginning the process of finding the broadest possible claim and useful in inventor meetings when inventors are unfamiliar with claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be supported by the description and drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be supported by the description. The detailed description should breathe life into the claims and provide a sufficient disclosure so that a skilled person could make & understand the invention. If a highly abstract term is used in the claims, the same term should be used in the detailed description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure every claim has adequate support in the specification; verify drawings and description after finalizing claim set so claim terms are appropriately described and defined; provide sufficient depth to allow narrowing during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include claims of varying scope (broad and narrow)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include both broad and narrow claims; consider claim sets of varying scope rather than only an independent claim followed by narrower dependents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad claims catch a wider group of infringers, narrow claims are more likely to be valid over unknown prior art — provide the client with both options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create dependent claims from features removed to achieve breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: Often the patent agent can prepare dependent claims from things removed from draft claims while writing broad claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be creative when choosing which features to remove for broad independent claims so those features can be recaptured as dependent claims to maximize protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must define the invention, be clear and concise, and be drafted in technical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Claims must: define the invention for which protection is being sought, be clear and concise, be supported by the description and drawings, and be drafted in terms of technical features of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague or non-technical language in claim elements; focus on technical features that will be used to assess novelty/inventive step and infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful choice of words to capture invention and variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Words should capture the invention as well as variants; word meanings must be appropriate and must convey meaning and cover the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose terminology that covers foreseeable variants; ensure the wording will be interpreted to include intended alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous relative adjectives unless relationally defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch out for “relative” words like fast, slow, long, short, tall, wide, perfect, complete, thin, strong, flat, etc., unless the relationship lies with another recited element in the claim (e.g., “wherein the first piece is shorter than the second piece”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using relative terms, explicitly define the relationship between claim elements or quantify where possible to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain field-specific terms and define new terms
rubrics_metrics.description: If you use a word established in a given technical field, make sure you understand what the word means and doesn’t mean. Explain the word’s meaning in the description if necessary. If you use a new word in the claims, then make sure that you clearly establish its meaning in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume uniform understanding across jurisdictions; explicitly define novel terms to avoid indefiniteness or misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid negative limitations; prefer positive phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid negative limitations in claims (e.g., “a tire that is not solid”); state limitations in positive terms (e.g., “a hollow tire”) unless the limitation cannot be phrased in any other manner (e.g., “a non-black color”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive limitations are clearer and easier to enforce; use negatives only when unavoidable and supported by the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure consistency and adequate support of claim language in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure every claim has adequate support in the specification; words and terminology should be consistent. You don’t need to define terms already known in the industry if using them consistent with industry practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check each claim element against the detailed description and drawings; inconsistent terminology can create vulnerabilities to invalidity or enablement objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate competitors and potential workarounds; draft alternative embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Think about variations or other embodiments of the invention; think like a potential competitor trying to avoid the patent; assume the competitor has prior art that can knock out your broadest claim; incorporate alternative embodiments into the description and claim them to broaden protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include fallback embodiments in the specification and claim a range of alternatives so competitors cannot easily design around the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary limitations; file broadest patentable independent claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Delete all unnecessary limitations before filing claims. File only the limitations or essential technical features necessary to recite the invention in its broadest patentable form in the broadest independent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trim superfluous detail from independent claims to preserve breadth; reserve non-essential features for dependent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance claiming breadth with overcoming prior art and validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should, if possible, cover competing products but must overcome the prior art. Be aware of related prior art; do not file claims that you know to be invalid. Ideally draft a claim narrower than prior art but broader than competing (non‑prior‑art) products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search and analyze prior art before choosing claim scope; tailor claims to maximize enforceability while covering competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple claim categories (device/method/uses) judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple claim categories for the same invention to get the broadest possible protection — some competitors will infringe device claims but not method claims and vice versa. Don’t include every type of claim just for inclusiveness — use your judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims in different statutory categories where appropriate (e.g., apparatus, method, use) but avoid unnecessary or unsupported claim types that complicate prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider who the infringer will be when drafting claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Always think about who is the infringer — DON’T MAKE YOUR CUSTOMER THE ONLY POSSIBLE INFRINGER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to capture likely infringers (manufacturers, sellers, users) rather than only end customers, to improve enforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowing during prosecution must be supported by the original description and done with minimal harm
rubrics_metrics.description: To narrow a patent claim during prosecution, add new elements to the claims and/or add new limitations to existing elements. All new additions must be supported by the description as filed. Consider all relevant options when amending a claim and do the least harm possible. The client should understand the implications of any claim amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning possible amendments, ensure fallback language exists in the original filing; discuss prosecution strategy and tradeoffs with the client.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of statutory exclusions and draft around them
rubrics_metrics.description: Most jurisdictions explicitly exclude certain types of inventions from patenting. The patent agent can sometimes simply re-word a claim to bring it from an unacceptable invention class to an acceptable one. TIP: Be prepared to fight for the patentability of certain types of inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze jurisdictional exclusion rules (e.g., biotech, medical methods) early and consider alternative claim formats or arguments to avoid exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use alternative claim formats (e.g., Swiss‑type, medical use) to circumvent exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: In jurisdictions where methods of treating the human body are excluded, use alternative claim formats such as "Compound X for use in a method for treating diabetes" (Swiss‑type) or "Use of compound X in the manufacture of a medicament for the treatment of diabetes" (medical use claim) to obtain protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select jurisdiction‑appropriate claim formulations for subject matter that faces exclusion; cite examples where these formats have been used to obtain protection in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include at least one claim that reads on the client’s actual activities/products
rubrics_metrics.description: At least one claim in the application should read on what the client is actually doing. Defending the client’s products against infringement may be difficult otherwise; patent marking is also difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure practical enforceability by including claim language that covers the client’s real-world product(s) or methods so they can rely on the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft claims early to identify specification requirements and define terms
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claims are prepared before drafting the specification, the patent agent knows precisely which terms need to be described clearly in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use early claim drafts to guide the detailed description and drawings; this reduces the risk of missing support for claim terms and facilitates later amendments.
